name: Spreader grafts
lead: Spreader grafts are thin strips of cartilage, usually taken from the nasal septum, that surgeons place between the septum and the upper lateral cartilages during rhinoplasty. They are used to widen the internal nasal valve, support or straighten the middle third of the nose, and keep the dorsal aesthetic lines smooth after a dorsal hump has been reduced [1][2][9].

Reduction of a dorsal hump often disrupts the junction of the septum and upper lateral cartilages (sometimes called the keystone area), and surgeons describe spreader grafts or spreader flaps as ways to rebuild it for both appearance and breathing [1]. Surgeons also publish techniques intended to lessen the need for them, such as component dorsal reduction that preserves the upper lateral cartilages [2].

Published evidence consists mainly of surgeon case series and technique descriptions. At least one registered randomized trial has compared outcomes with and without spreader grafts in reduction rhinoseptoplasty with a quality-of-life measure, but its results are not published in the sources reviewed here [3].

paras: The internal nasal valve is the narrowest part of the nasal airway, bounded by the septum and the caudal edge of the upper lateral cartilage. Surgeons have long investigated valve incompetence as a contributor to airway obstruction alongside septal deviation [4][5]. A spreader graft is a rectangular cartilage strip fixed on one or both sides of the dorsal septum so that the upper lateral cartilages are held apart from it [9].

Variants described in the literature include alar spreader grafts, proposed for a pinched nasal tip [6], the upper lateral splay graft [7], and the spreader flap, in which the upper lateral cartilage itself is folded inward rather than a separate graft being used [3][8]. General rhinoplasty references also note that spreader grafts, often combined with flaring sutures, are used when the internal valve is too narrow [9].

Spreader grafts are used to treat nasal obstruction attributed to internal valve narrowing or collapse. A cadaver and clinical study of surgery for the dysfunctional nasal valve reported outcomes of valve-directed procedures [5], and a study of 160 primary and secondary rhinoplasty patients compared the relative contribution of septal and valve surgery to airway improvement [4].

After hump reduction, surgeons use grafts or flaps to avoid an inverted-V deformity, dorsal irregularities, and a narrowed middle vault, and the surgeon who described component dorsal reduction notes that preserving the upper lateral cartilages can reduce how often spreader grafts are needed in primary cases [2]. They are also used in correcting a crooked nose, where straightening the septum and dorsum is a recurring difficulty and revision rates are described as fairly high [10].

Dorsal preservation techniques aim to lower the dorsum without removing the hump and cutting the keystone area. One surgeon's series of 320 cases over five years described a push-down technique and noted that most conventional reduction operations destroy the keystone area and therefore require reconstruction [1]. Spreader flaps are presented as an alternative that uses the patient's own upper lateral cartilage [8].

A registered randomized trial (NCT04499469, 50 participants, started in 2018) examines the role of spreader grafts in reduction rhinoseptoplasty with a quality-of-life assessment; its status is listed as unknown and no results were found [3]. A second registered study (NCT01852643, 50 participants, completed) compared a spreader graft with a lateral crural overlay technique [11]. Most published literature is retrospective surgeon experience, including the cadaver and clinical valve study and a 160-patient series on airway outcomes [4][5].

Spreader grafts are placed as part of rhinoplasty, which carries general surgical risks. Rhinoplasty references report that revision surgery accounts for roughly 5 to 20 percent of operations and that swelling can take a year or more to resolve [9]. Specific complication rates for spreader grafts alone were not reported in the sources reviewed.

card.summary: Cartilage strips placed beside the septum to open the internal nasal valve and keep the nose bridge straight after hump reduction; supported mainly by surgeon case series.
card.note: Part of rhinoplasty; revision surgery is reported in roughly 5 to 20 percent of rhinoplasties.

quick.overview:
Spreader grafts are small strips of cartilage, usually from the septum, placed along the nasal bridge during rhinoplasty. Surgeons use them to widen the internal nasal valve, keep the bridge straight and avoid a pinched mid-nose after a hump is reduced.

The evidence is mostly surgeon case series and technique papers, with a few registered trials.
quick.mechanism: The graft holds the upper lateral cartilages away from the septum, widening the angle of the internal nasal valve and preserving smooth dorsal lines.
quick.risks: It is done under general rhinoplasty risks, and revision rhinoplasty accounts for roughly 5 to 20 percent of cases. Graft-specific complication rates were not reported in the sources reviewed. It is a surgical procedure performed only by clinicians.
